scenes.say: You keep hearing about Docker images and containers. But what's the difference, and why does it matter?

scenes.label: Image
scenes.sub: A read-only template, built in layers.
scenes.say: A Docker image is a read-only template, built up in layers. Think of it like a golden master copy.

scenes.label: Container
scenes.sub: A running instance with its own writable layer.
scenes.say: A container is a running instance of an image. It gets its own thin writable layer on top, so it can change files as it runs.

scenes.code:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
# Now you're in a container
scenes.say: When you run an image, Docker creates a container. Now you can write files, install packages, and run commands—just in your container.
Images are reusable, read-only templates. Containers are live, writable, and ephemeral—meaning they vanish when stopped unless you save data outside.

scenes.question: Can you edit an image by running a container?
scenes.right: No—changes stay in the container's writable layer. The image itself never changes.
scenes.say: Interview trap: You can't edit an image by running a container. Changes only live in the container's writable layer, not the image.
